subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Polyhydramnios, Oligohydramnios, AFI and Deepest Pool

steps.tx: Excess amniotic fluid, deepest pool over eight centimetres or index over twenty five, is **polyhydramnios**. Diabetes, fetal anomalies and twin transfusion head the cause list. Breathlessness and discomfort mark severe acute cases. Mild cases sit at an index of 25 to 29.9, moderate 30 to 34.9, and severe at 35 or above.
steps.say: Polyhydramnios exceeds normal fluid from diabetes, anomalies or twin transfusion.

steps.tx: Too little fluid, deepest pool under two centimetres, is **oligohydramnios**. Ruptured membranes, growth restriction and renal anomalies cause it. The fetus is at risk of cord compression and, early, lung hypoplasia. Duration matters: fluid absent for over two weeks before 26 weeks carries the worst lung prognosis.
steps.say: Oligohydramnios falls below two centimetres from rupture, restriction or renal anomalies.

steps.tx: Summing deepest pools from four uterine quadrants gives the **amniotic fluid index**. It quantifies fluid for surveillance trends. Technique variation is wide, so trends by the same method matter most. Measuring the cord free pools avoids counting pockets that contain cord or fetal parts.
steps.say: The amniotic fluid index sums four quadrant pools for surveillance trends.

steps.tx: The single largest vertical pocket, preferred by many for fewer interventions, is the **single deepest pocket**. It labels fewer pregnancies abnormal than the index with similar outcomes. Either method must be used consistently. Depth of 2 to 8 centimetres is normal; below 2 is low and above 8 is excess by this method.
steps.say: The single deepest pocket labels fewer pregnancies abnormal with similar outcomes.

steps.tx: Failed swallowing from blocked oesophagus causes fluid excess, as in **oesophageal atresia**. The fetal stomach bubble is absent on scan. Polyhydramnios is often the first antenatal clue to this anomaly. Diabetic polyhydramnios from fetal polyuria is the main alternative when the stomach bubble is seen normally.
steps.say: Oesophageal atresia blocks swallowing, causing polyhydramnios with an absent stomach bubble.

steps.tx: Absent cranial vault prevents normal swallowing and fluid regulation in **anencephaly**. It is a classic polyhydramnios association detectable at the first trimester scan. The diagnosis is lethal and counselling follows local law and family wishes. Associated polyhydramnios comes from failure to swallow plus excess urine from the high output state.
steps.say: Anencephaly impairs swallowing and causes polyhydramnios detectable in the first trimester.

steps.tx: Absent kidneys abolish fetal urine and fluid in bilateral **renal agenesis**. This lethal condition produces the Potter sequence of compressed facies and hypoplastic lungs. It is the extreme end of oligohydramnios causation. Other causes include posterior urethral valves with late failure and prolonged rupture of membranes.
steps.say: Renal agenesis abolishes urine and fluid, producing the lethal Potter sequence.

steps.tx: Idiopathic cases with no cause found form the majority of mild polyhydramnios, termed **idiopathic polyhydramnios**. Even these carry slightly raised preterm and malpresentation risks. Glucose screening and anomaly review still complete the workup. Macrosomia screening matters because glucose driven growth hides among the apparently idiopathic cases.
steps.say: Idiopathic polyhydramnios still needs glucose screening and anomaly review.

steps.tx: Acute polyhydramnios over days causes severe maternal breathlessness needing **amnioreduction**. Slow removal of one to two litres by amniocentesis relieves symptoms. It recurs while the cause persists, so it palliates rather than cures. Fluid is withdrawn slowly and stopped if the mother becomes hypotensive or the fetal heart falters.
steps.say: Amnioreduction slowly removes fluid to relieve breathlessness in acute polyhydramnios.
